summary: Extends HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery so a location request can identify the device, not rely only on the source IP address. This helps where the address does not map directly to a device's location. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This document lets a location request name the device it is about, using an IP address, a MAC address, a network login name or one of several other identifiers. That is needed when the source address is not enough, or when someone other than the device asks for its location.

subtitle: Lets a location request name the device it is about, instead of relying only on the source IP address.

tldr.problem: A location server normally works out who is asking from the source IP address of the request, which is enough only when the address maps directly to one device.
tldr.mechanism: The document extends HELD so a request can carry device identifiers in an XML device element, and defines which identifiers may be used, when they are safe, and how the server must authorize the requestor.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard from March 2011, updated by RFC 6915, and it moves HELD outside the simpler model where a device asking for its own location is trusted automatically.

today: RFC 6155 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2011. It is updated by RFC 6915 and has not been obsoleted, so the device identity elements it defines remain part of HELD.

sections.title: Why a Location Request Needs Identity
sections.content:
Protocols that deliver location information need some way for the requester to say whose location is wanted. In a Location Configuration Protocol (LCP) the location being requested is the requester's own, and that makes the problem simple: the IP datagram carrying the request already identifies the device, because the source IP address is right there in the packet. Existing LCPs, including HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery (HELD) in RFC 5985 and the DHCP options in RFC 3825 and RFC 4776, rely on the source address or other information present in the packet datagrams.

This document changes that. It extends HELD so that a request can carry explicit device identifiers in the body of the message, and it defines an XML schema for them. Two use cases motivate the work: location configuration that needs an identifier other than the source IP address, and a request made by someone other than the device whose location is wanted, which the document calls a third-party location recipient.

One characteristic matters. HELD with identity extensions is not an LCP. An LCP covers only the interaction between a device and a location server, so the server can guarantee the device's identity from the source address and from the check that the address is not spoofed. Once a requestor can name the device in the message body, that guarantee is gone, so the server has to authorize the requestor explicitly.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a device asks a server for its own location, and the server can tell who is asking from the network address in the request. This document lets the request name the device instead, which is needed when the address is not enough or when someone else is asking.

sections.title: When an Identifier Is Good Enough
sections.content:
An identifier is only usable if it points to exactly one device at the moment the location is worked out. The location server is responsible for that, because it is the one answering. An identifier that is temporary, or that could point at more than one device, can be used by an attacker to learn about another device or to make the server produce misleading information.

Two problems get their own subsections. Subjective network views arise because each network entity has its own view of the network, so the same identifier can mean different physical things in different contexts. This is especially true of IP addresses. Network address translation and other forms of address modification create these separate contexts, and private use addresses are the most obvious identifiers with limited scope. Unless the third party and the server share a network context, the location returned is correct only in the server's context and is probably misleading to the requester. A server can be configured to recognise such cases and either adjust the answer or reject the request.

Transient identifiers are ones that get reassigned to different physical entities over time. If an identifier is reassigned between the moment the requester forms the request and the moment the server receives it, the server locates a different entity from the one intended, even though the answer it sends is accurate. A server should know which identifiers may be temporary, and must not provide location information if the identifier might refer to a different device.

A third point concerns interfaces. Several of the identifiers name a network interface rather than a whole device. Uniquely identifying any interface is assumed to be enough, on the grounds that the goal is to find the device attached to that interface.
sections.plainLanguage: An identifier is only safe if it points at one device and one device only. Identifiers that get reused, or that mean different things on different networks, can give the wrong answer or expose another device's location.

sections.title: The device Element in a HELD Request
sections.content:
XML elements carry the device identity. The device element is a general container, and the identifiers live in their own XML namespace, urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:geopriv:held:id. The basic identity schema allows elements from any namespace, so other namespaces can add identifiers of their own.

A server that supports this specification echoes the device element in a successful response, including the identifiers it actually used as the basis for location determination. If the element is absent from the response, the location was generated from the source IP address in the request instead.

Two error paths are defined. A badIdentifier error code means the requestor is not authorized to use that identifier, or that the identifier is badly formatted or not supported by the server. When the server needs an identifier the request did not carry, it MAY name the identifiers it requires with the requiredIdentifiers element, which holds a list of XML qualified names such as mac and ip, with namespace prefixes taken from the surrounding document.
sections.plainLanguage: The device goes in the request body as an XML element. The server repeats back the identifiers it used, so the requester can tell which ones the answer was based on.

sections.title: The Identifiers the Document Defines
sections.content:
The document defines a set of identifiers. An IP address is carried in an ip element whose v attribute gives the IP version as a single hexadecimal digit, using the textual format for that version. A MAC address appears in a mac element as MAC-48, EUI-48 or EUI-64 in hexadecimal, and it identifies the device using that interface as long as the two stay together. A locally assigned MAC address is only unique inside the domain where it was assigned.

Port numbers are carried in udpport, tcpport, sctpport and dccpport elements. A port number on its own cannot identify a host, but combined with an IP address it can in some circumstances, which matters because network address translation means some devices cannot be identified by address alone.

A Network Access Identifier, the user identity used in network authentication, goes in an nai element. Because the formal grammar permits octet sequences that are not valid UTF-8, the XML form allows an escape, a backslash followed by two hexadecimal digits standing for one octet. A URI goes in a uri element, and care is needed because a URI can resolve to several destinations, for example a SIP address of record that stands for a service subscription. A fully qualified domain name goes in an fqdn element, though a name that covers several hosts is not a suitable identifier.

The cellular telephony identifiers are msisdn, imsi, imei, min and mdn, each a string of decimal digits. The MSISDN is an E.164 number of 6 to 15 digits, the IMSI is between 6 and 15 digits, the IMEI is a device serial number of up to 15 digits, and the MIN is a 10-digit number assigned to CDMA handsets. The DHCP Unique Identifier goes in a duid element as the binary value written in hexadecimal.
sections.plainLanguage: The document lists the kinds of identifier a request may carry: an IP address, a MAC address, a port number, a network login name, a URI, a domain name, mobile phone numbers, and the identifier DHCP gives a device.

sections.title: Checking an NAI in a WiMAX Network
sections.content:
One identifier comes with a defined way of proving that the requester and the named device are the same. In a WiMAX network a Network Access Identifier is uniquely attributable to a single device at any one time, because an NAI identifies either a device or a service subscription, and neither can have more than one active session. An IP address is not enough for a server in that network, so location requests there always include an NAI.

The procedure runs like this. If the request does not come from an authenticated and authorized third-party requestor, the server may treat it as a location configuration request. On receiving a request that includes an NAI, the server sends a "Location-Requestor-Authentication-Protocol" access request message to the Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) server, carrying the NAI in an "MS-Identity-Assertion" parameter. The AAA server consults network policy and, if the request is permitted, answers with the IP address currently assigned to the device. If that address matches the source IP address of the HELD location request, the request can be authorized under the LCP policy; otherwise the request must be treated as a third-party request.

The procedure relies on the same protections against IP address spoofing that RFC 5985 requires, and on the protections of the AAA protocol, which is either Diameter (RFC 3588) or RADIUS (RFC 2865). The AAA server MUST be authenticated as a trusted entity for the purpose of linking the NAI to the IP address, and the AAA protocol MUST protect against modification and replay attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: In a WiMAX network, the server can check with the network's own login system whether the device named in the request is the one that sent it. That check needs the login system to be trusted and the traffic between them to be protected.

sections.title: Who May Ask for a Location
sections.content:
Location configuration protocols use a simple authorization model, the "LCP policy", which permits only the target to receive its own location. The security and privacy rules of the base HELD protocol still apply, but the return routability check does not apply to third-party requests, and may not apply to a target asking for its own location either, depending on the anti-spoofing mechanism used for the identifier.

When a target uses the identity extensions to get its own location, HELD is no longer an LCP, so the policy the server applies must come from one or more rule makers. If the server gives only targets their own locations it can still be said to follow the LCP policy, but the spoofing protections differ: for an LCP, return routability is enough, so a similar policy needs specific measures to prevent spoofing of the alternative identifier. The document defines those measures for the NAI in WiMAX networks and for no other identifier. Where identifiers are not uniquely attributable to a single device, for example when several devices with different MAC addresses share one NAI, the same protections do not hold.

Third-party requests are stricter still. The LCP policy does not allow them, so a server that permits them takes on the role of a location server and MUST authorize each request according to policies set by rule makers, including the target, and MUST authenticate the requestor. Until an authorization policy is in place the server MUST reject third-party requests, so the default is deny all. The document does not mandate a mechanism for establishing that policy, but points to access control lists, to terms of service, or to automated policy documents such as the common policy format in RFC 4745.
sections.plainLanguage: A device asking for its own location can be trusted fairly easily. Someone else asking needs permission that was set up in advance, and until that permission exists the server must refuse.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The base HELD protocol uses Transport Layer Security (RFC 5246) for server authentication, confidentiality and protection from modification, and those protections apply both to target requests and to third-party requests. On top of that, all HELD requests containing identity MUST be authenticated by the server, and how that is done is a matter of policy. The base protocol treats the ability of a requester to complete a TCP handshake as proof of return reachability of its IP address, and any authentication method is RECOMMENDED to provide at least that much assurance. For requests that include device identity, the requester MUST support HTTP digest authentication (RFC 2617), and an unauthenticated request with identity may be challenged with an HTTP 401 response or rejected with an HTTP 403 response. Since base HELD does not require devices to implement authentication, a server SHOULD NOT send a 401 to a device that did not include device identity.

Transient and ambiguous identifiers can be exploited, as Section 2.1 sets out. An attacker who knows of a re-allocation, or who can force one during the processing of a request, could obtain the location of another device, or make the server lie, if the re-allocation happens between the moment authorization is granted and the moment location information is granted. An ambiguous identifier is dangerous in a similar way, because authorization granted for one of the devices it might refer to can give access to all of them.

Privacy is called out separately. Identity information a device supplies is private data that might be sensitive, and the server MUST NOT use it for any purpose other than serving the request that carried it.
sections.plainLanguage: Requests that name a device must be authenticated, and the server must use the identity only for that request. Identifiers that get reused are an obvious way to trick a server into giving out the wrong location.
